stem: An organisation's awareness training was written when all staff worked in the office. Half now work from home or from shared spaces. Which gap is most likely?

options.text: It assumes a controlled perimeter, so it omits home network security, shared workspace shoulder surfing and household device separation
options.why: Hybrid and remote work is listed as its own topic because the assumptions change: there is no reception desk, no corporate network, and often no private space.

options.text: It will overemphasise phishing, which is less relevant remotely
options.why: Phishing is at least as relevant remotely, since there is no colleague nearby to sanity check a suspicious message.

options.text: It cannot cover password management for remote staff
options.why: Password management applies identically wherever someone works.

options.text: Remote staff do not require awareness training because they use managed devices
options.why: A managed device does not make judgement calls about a convincing phone call or an overlooked screen.

stem: A caller claiming to be from the IT service desk pressures a finance assistant to read back a one-time code, citing an urgent outage. Which awareness topic addresses this most directly?

options.text: Social engineering awareness, which trains recognition of urgency, authority and pretext
options.why: No technical control intercepts a persuasive phone call. The defence is the person recognising the pattern and having a sanctioned way to refuse.

options.text: Password management
options.why: Concerns how credentials are chosen and stored, not how someone is talked out of one.

options.text: Removable media and cables
options.why: Covers physical media brought into the environment.

options.text: Operational security
options.why: Concerns what staff disclose publicly about systems and roles, which can enable the pretext but is not the moment described.

stem: An engineer's conference talk names the organisation's EDR product, its SIEM, its cloud provider and its patch cadence. Which awareness topic does this concern?

options.text: Operational security: limiting what is publicly disclosed about systems, tooling and process
options.why: Each detail narrows an attacker's work. OPSEC is about controlling the information an adversary would otherwise have to discover.

options.text: Insider threat awareness
options.why: Nothing suggests malice or a concerning pattern of behaviour. This is an unintentional disclosure.

options.text: Situational awareness
options.why: That concerns noticing what is happening around you physically, such as tailgating or shoulder surfing.

options.text: Policy handbooks
options.why: A handbook might prohibit it; the topic the behaviour belongs to is operational security.

stem: Why do awareness programmes require staff to acknowledge policy handbooks rather than simply publishing them?

options.text: Acknowledgement records that the individual was informed, which is what makes the expectation enforceable and the training auditable
options.why: A rule nobody has read cannot reasonably be enforced. The acknowledgement is the evidence that converts a published document into an expectation.

options.text: Because acknowledgement guarantees the policy has been understood
options.why: It records receipt, not comprehension, which is why training sits alongside it rather than being replaced by it.

options.text: Because handbooks are a technical control
options.why: They are directive administrative controls.

options.text: Because regulators require a signature on every policy
options.why: Requirements vary and the underlying purpose is enforceability and evidence.

stem: An organisation deploys a password manager and sets a strong policy, yet reuse of work passwords on personal sites continues. What does the awareness programme need to address?

options.text: Password management behaviour: why reuse across sites is dangerous, and how to use the manager for personal accounts too
options.why: Policy governs what the corporate system accepts. Reuse happens outside it, which is exactly the space awareness has to reach.

options.text: Nothing further; the technical control has solved it
options.why: The control cannot see or prevent what staff do on sites it does not govern.

options.text: Social engineering awareness
options.why: Relevant to credential theft by manipulation, not to voluntary reuse.

options.text: Operational security
options.why: Concerns public disclosure of information about systems.

stem: Staff return from a trade event with branded USB drives and charging cables. Which awareness topic covers the risk, and why is training needed when port control exists?

options.text: Removable media and cables; port control reduces but does not eliminate the paths, and staff decide what they carry in and what they plug into personal equipment
options.why: Cables are named specifically because people who would refuse an unknown drive will happily accept a cable. Technical controls cover some ports, not every decision.

options.text: Insider threat awareness, since staff introduced the devices
options.why: That topic concerns recognising and reporting concerning behaviour, not accidental introduction of hardware.

options.text: Policy handbooks alone are sufficient here
options.why: A written rule without training is the situation that produces this behaviour.

options.text: Hybrid and remote work environments
options.why: Relevant where staff work, not to hardware collected at an event.

stem: Why is insider threat awareness a training topic for ordinary staff rather than only for security teams?

options.text: Colleagues see context that monitoring cannot: escalating grievance, unusual interest in systems outside a role, or pressure that might make someone a target
options.why: Technical monitoring observes actions. The surrounding circumstances that make an action meaningful are visible to the people nearby, which is why the reporting route matters.

options.text: Because all staff should be treated as suspects
options.why: The topic is recognising and reporting concerning indicators, including coercion of a colleague, not generalised suspicion.

options.text: Because insider threats are always malicious
options.why: Insider risk also includes unintentional and risky behaviour; negligence is a large share of insider incidents.

options.text: Because it replaces the need for user behaviour analytics
options.why: They complement each other: UBA sees the pattern in the data, colleagues see the situation around it.

stem: Which TWO statements about security awareness programmes are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Awareness targets the part of the attack surface where a person makes a judgement, which technical controls cannot reach
options.why: No filter intercepts a persuasive phone call, and no policy decides what someone does on a site it does not govern.

options.text: Hybrid and remote working needs its own treatment because office-based training assumes a perimeter that is not there
options.why: It is listed as its own topic for this reason: home networks, shared spaces and household devices are different assumptions.

options.text: Acknowledging a policy handbook demonstrates that staff understood it
options.why: It records that they were informed. Understanding is what the training is for.

options.text: Deploying a password manager removes the need to train password behaviour
options.why: The tool cannot govern accounts outside it, which is where reuse happens.

options.text: Insider threat awareness is only relevant to the security team
options.why: Colleagues observe the context that monitoring cannot.

stem: A phishing simulation shows a low click rate, but almost nobody reports the simulated messages. What should the security team conclude?

options.text: Reporting is the weak point, and the programme should make reporting easy and recognised
options.why: Someone will eventually click. What determines the outcome is how quickly the security team hears about it, so report rate is the more useful measure.

options.text: The programme is effective, since the click rate is what matters
options.why: Click rate measures the attack's success. It says nothing about whether your organisation can detect and respond.

options.text: The simulation was too easy and should be made harder before anything else
options.why: Difficulty tuning is worth doing and does not address the finding, which is that nobody is reporting.

options.text: Users who failed to report should be formally disciplined
options.why: Punishment suppresses reporting. The reliable way to raise report rates is to make reporting frictionless and to recognise people who do it.

stem: Which combination best describes an effective security awareness programme?

options.text: Initial training at onboarding plus recurring training with refreshed content, and targeted follow-up for users who need it
options.why: New starters are trained immediately, everyone is trained repeatedly, the content changes so it is not ignored, and weak spots get specific attention.

options.text: A single comprehensive session at onboarding
options.why: Without recurring training, knowledge decays and new threats are never covered.

options.text: An annual repeat of the same training deck for everyone
options.why: Recurring is right and unchanged content trains people to click through without reading.

options.text: Publishing the acceptable use policy on the intranet
options.why: Making a policy available is not training and does not change behaviour.

stem: A user emails a customer spreadsheet to their personal address so they can finish work at the weekend. How is this behaviour best characterised?

options.text: Risky but unintentional, and best addressed with guidance and a sanctioned alternative
options.why: There is no malicious intent. The user has a legitimate need and no approved way to meet it, so the fix is training plus a usable remote access route.

options.text: A malicious insider threat requiring immediate termination
options.why: Nothing indicates intent to harm. Treating well meant shortcuts as malice destroys the reporting culture you depend on.

options.text: Acceptable, since the user is working in the company's interest
options.why: Good intent does not make it acceptable. Customer data has left the organisation's control entirely.

options.text: A technical control failure only, with no behavioural component
options.why: DLP should have caught it, and the behaviour still needs addressing, or the user finds the next workaround.

stem: A user reports a suspicious message that turns out to be the monthly phishing simulation. What should the awareness programme do?

options.text: Thank the user and confirm the report was correct, so reporting is reinforced
options.why: The report is the behaviour the programme wants. Prompt, positive feedback makes the next report more likely, including the one that is real.

options.text: Ignore it, because it was only a simulation
options.why: A correct report was made and then met with silence. People learn that reporting changes nothing.

options.text: Tell the user that reporting simulations wastes analyst time
options.why: That discourages the exact behaviour being trained, and a real attack is indistinguishable from a simulation to the user.

options.text: Record a mark against the user for reporting a test message
options.why: Penalising a correct report suppresses reporting, which destroys the measure that matters.

stem: An employee repeatedly uses a personal file sharing account for work documents because the approved tool is slow. How should the programme classify and treat this?

options.text: Risky but unintentional, treated with guidance and a usable sanctioned alternative
options.why: There is no intent to harm. The behaviour persists because the approved path is worse, so training alone will not change it.

options.text: Malicious insider activity, treated as a disciplinary matter
options.why: Nothing indicates intent to harm. Treating well-meant shortcuts as malice ends the reporting culture you depend on.

options.text: Acceptable, since productivity improved
options.why: Company documents have left the organisation's control. Good intent does not make that acceptable.

options.text: Purely a technical failure, treated by blocking the service
options.why: Blocking without fixing the slow approved tool simply moves the behaviour to the next workaround.

stem: A company trains new starters thoroughly at onboarding and never again. What is the gap?

options.text: No recurring training, so knowledge decays and new threats are never covered
options.why: Awareness has an initial and a recurring component. Onboarding alone leaves everyone hired more than a year ago on out of date material.

options.text: No initial training
options.why: Initial training is the part they do have.

options.text: Training should be replaced by technical controls
options.why: Controls and awareness address different failure modes. Neither replaces the other.

options.text: Nothing, provided the onboarding module is comprehensive
options.why: No module survives contact with a threat landscape that changes after it was recorded.

stem: At a conference venue, a stranger follows a staff member through a badge-controlled door into the back office corridor. Which awareness topic covers the habit of noticing and challenging this?

options.text: Situational awareness
options.why: It is about noticing what is happening around you physically, such as tailgating, and acting on it rather than assuming someone else will.

options.text: Phishing recognition
options.why: Phishing arrives as a message. This is a person physically entering a controlled area.

options.text: Password management
options.why: Unrelated to the behaviour described.

options.text: Hybrid and remote work
options.why: That topic covers the different assumptions of working away from the office, such as home networks. It does not describe challenging an unknown person at a door.
